children: Investments in biomedical startups can take more than a decade to pay off. The structure of the new $410 million venture fund from life-sciences investor Luma Group reflects that and a bit more.
Most venture-capital funds are 10-year limited partnerships, so investors expect their money back, plus profits, in that time frame, though extensions can be granted.

New York-based Luma instead structured its fund, LumaBio I LP, as a 15-year vehicle so it can hold investments longer and, potentially, reap greater paydays by exiting its positions when portfolio companies are more mature and more highly valued. Managing Member Josh Fink and General Partner Themasap Khan founded Luma Group.
Fink said the team put a great deal of thought into the fund structure and decided it should align with the long timelines companies often need to advance new treatments.

Luma doesn't need to hold investments for 15 years, but the team likes having the option to do so, Khan said. The approach could be thought of as a middle ground between a 10-year venture fund and an evergreen.
"We want to have the duration necessary to really see through some of the most important therapies and not have a fund that's prematurely cut short," Fink said.

The structure is unusual, and some prospective investors said a 15-year structure was too long. But, after three years of fundraising, Luma collected a group of limited partners who agreed with its vision, among them insurers, family offices, sovereign-wealth funds and individuals.
"It allows us the patience to make the best decisions when the time is right," said Khan.

Biotech venture investment is recovering from its postpandemic slide, as both initial public offerings and mergers and acquisitions pick up. But when Luma Group launched in 2023, biotech was in a slump.

Luma launched the fund with a conviction that advances in biology and computation would lead to revolutionary new drugs, diagnostics and medical devices, and that investor pullback hadn't dimmed that opportunity.

In late 2024, the firm became an early investor in Vaccine Company, whose pipeline included a potential prophylactic vaccine for Epstein-Barr virus, which can cause illnesses including infectious mononucleosis.

Venture capitalists' interest in vaccines rose during the pandemic, but many investors moved on after the crisis ended. The Luma team saw significant unmet need remaining in the field and recognized that vaccines are crucial products to many pharmaceutical companies, Fink said. In May, drugmaker Eli Lilly agreed to buy Vaccine Company for up to $1.55 billion-the first exit for Luma's fund. The acquisition closed over the summer.

Luma, which typically seeks to lead or co-lead investments, has a partner, Jamie Kasuboski, who heads an effort to scour scientific literature and analyze emerging fields. That research yields insights into new investment opportunities, when to invest in a field and when to exit, Fink said.

Luma's debut fund had an initial closing in July 2023 and wrapped up fundraising in July of this year, Fink said. So far, the fund has invested in nine companies and expects to back about 15 in total. That includes some that the firm launches itself, Khan said.
